The Sin croaker Johnius dussumieri is a commercially important sciaenid found along the Indian coast, and recent studies have clarified several aspects of its life history. Field estimates indicate that females first attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 11.5 cm [Lp = 11.5 cm], a size threshold that likely corresponds to approximately one year of age in this region. The ultimate total length for this species has been recorded at 40 cm [Li = 40 cm], although individuals exceeding 35 cm are uncommon in trawl catches, suggesting high fishing pressure on larger size classes. At the onset of puberty, the average wet weight of an individual is approximately 15 grams [Wwp = approximately 15 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions developed for local populations. This modest body mass at maturation contrasts with the considerably larger sizes achieved later in life, reflecting a life-history strategy common among sciaenids that prioritize body growth before reaching reproductive age.

Under the stable thermal conditions prevailing in the coastal waters where this species is commonly sampled, approximately 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], the maximum lifespan of J. dussumieri has been estimated at around 7,300 days [am = around 7,300 days] at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This longevity is relatively high compared to other small-bodied sciaenids and suggests a slow pace of life that may buffer the population against recruitment failures. The sustained high temperature also plays a crucial role in governing the species reproductive output. Under these conditions, field observations indicate that females produce approximately 415 eggs per event, calculated from annual fecundity estimates, and spawn approximately once per day. This fecundity of 415 eggs per event [N_R_i = 415 eggs per event] with a spawning frequency of once per day [F_R_i = spawning frequency of once per day] is among the highest documented for sciaenids of comparable body size and reflects a highly fecund, broadcast-spawning strategy typical of the family.

The pelagic eggs of Johnius dussumieri are notably small, with a diameter of approximately 1 millimeter. Based on this egg size and assuming spherical geometry, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00053 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00053 grams], a value typical of sciaenids that produce numerous, small, planktonic offspring. This minuscule initial mass poses significant challenges for the yolk-sac larva, which must rapidly develop feeding structures before exhausting its endogenous reserves. The chorionate embryo relies entirely on its yolk supply during the first few days after fertilization, and the timing of the transition to first exogenous feeding is critical for survival. Mortality during this early lecithotrophic stage is exceptionally high, with only a tiny fraction of the spawned eggs surviving to the juvenile stage. This high early mortality is offset by the tremendous fecundity of adult females, ensuring that enough recruits are produced each spawning season to maintain the population.

As individuals grow and mature, the relationship between length and mass becomes strongly allometric. The ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight regressions fitted to large adults, reaches approximately 686.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 686.4 grams] for fish attaining the maximum recorded total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm]. This asymptotic body mass is substantial for a sciaenid of this length and indicates a robust, deep-bodied morphology that confers a competitive advantage in benthic feeding. The species diet consists primarily of small crustaceans and polychaetes, and the energetic surplus from this high-protein diet supports both continued growth and the accumulation of gonadal reserves. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty of approximately 15 grams [Wwp = approximately 15 grams] is only about 2% of the ultimate mass, illustrating that reproductive maturation occurs relatively early in the life cycle, well before the individual has approached its maximum size.

Between the larval stage and the attainment of full maturity, Johnius dussumieri undergoes a dramatic increase in body mass, spanning several orders of magnitude. The wet weight of newly hatched larvae, at approximately 0.00053 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00053 grams], contrasts starkly with the several hundred grams of the adult fish, a difference that underscores the intense selective pressures acting on growth efficiency. The transition from the yolk-sac larva to the exogenously feeding juvenile is a particularly vulnerable period, during which the tiny prolarvae must successfully detect and capture their first prey before the remaining yolk is fully absorbed. Post-settlement juveniles, or fingerlings, settle in shallow, turbid inshore waters that offer both abundant food and refuge from larger piscivores. Growth during the first year is rapid, with individuals often reaching total lengths of 15 to 20 cm, enabling them to recruit into the adult feeding grounds.
